paragraphs.heading: Numbers that wrap around
paragraphs.text: Modular arithmetic is a way of doing sums with whole numbers in which the numbers wrap around once they reach or pass a chosen value. That value is called the modulus. To work modulo m, you take the result of each addition, subtraction or multiplication and swap it for the remainder left over after dividing by m.

paragraphs.heading: The clock on the wall
paragraphs.text: The hour hand of a 12-hour clock is the everyday case. If it points to 7 now, it points to 3 eight hours later. Plain addition gives 7 + 8 = 15, yet the clock face shows 3, since the hand goes round once every 12 hours and the numbering starts again after 12. We say 15 is congruent to 3 modulo 12 and write 15 ≡ 3 (mod 12).

paragraphs.heading: Twelve acts as zero
paragraphs.text: The same idea covers longer waits. Waiting 8 hours twice, 16 hours in all, moves the hand just as far as waiting 4 hours, which is written 2 × 8 ≡ 4 (mod 12). Wait exactly 12 hours and the hand is back where it began, so in this system 12 behaves like 0: 12 ≡ 0 (mod 12).

paragraphs.heading: Reading the notation
paragraphs.text: The statement a ≡ b (mod m) says that a and b leave the same remainder when divided by m. A different notation, b mod m, written without the parentheses, names that remainder itself: the single integer r with 0 ≤ r < m and r ≡ b (mod m). For example, 38 ≡ 14 (mod 12), because 38 − 14 = 24 = 2 × 12 is a multiple of 12. Put another way, both 38 and 14 leave remainder 2 when divided by 12.

paragraphs.heading: Reduce whenever you like
paragraphs.text: One handy property is that it does not matter when you divide by m. You can reduce after every step, only once at the very end, or now and then along the way, typically when a middle result grows too large. The final answer comes out the same.

paragraphs.heading: Division and inverses
paragraphs.text: A number a has a modular multiplicative inverse modulo m, written a⁻¹ and satisfying aa⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod m), exactly when a is coprime with m. With that inverse you can solve ax ≡ b (mod m): the answer is x ≡ a⁻¹b (mod m). The inverse can be computed efficiently with the extended Euclidean algorithm. When the modulus is a prime p, every a that is not congruent to 0 modulo p has an inverse.

paragraphs.heading: Famous results
paragraphs.text: Several theorems are stated in this language. Fermat's little theorem says that for a prime p that is not a divisor of a, aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p). The Chinese remainder theorem says that for coprime m and n, the two conditions x ≡ a (mod m) and x ≡ b (mod n) have a single solution x modulo mn. Carl Friedrich Gauss developed this modular approach to number theory in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, a book that appeared in 1801.
